Coach's note, inter-school innovation challenge, Team 3

After their water filter failed at the first trial, I expected the team to argue about blame. Instead, their captain, Amandeep, asked each of the five to name one concern about the next design, going round the circle. Nobody was allowed to pass.

Pooja, who had stayed silent in the first round, cleared her throat and said the charcoal layer was too thin. Another said the budget was nearly gone.

Amandeep then drew a table on the board with three columns: cost, time and how likely it was to work. The team scored three ideas out of five on each. The clay-pot filter scored lowest on cost and highest overall, though it was nobody's favourite at the start.

I watched them build it in eight days. It passed the second trial. I have asked Amandeep to explain the scoring table at our next club meeting.

qa.q: What were the three columns in Amandeep's table?
qa.a: Cost, time and how likely it was to work.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when she named her concern about the charcoal layer?
qa.a: Pooja probably felt nervous but relieved to finally speak, since she had stayed silent in the first round.

qa.q: What else could the team add to their decision process?
qa.a: They could agree to test the winning idea on a small scale first, so a scoring mistake shows up early.

qa.q: How does the new method look to the coach?
qa.a: The coach sees a team using evidence rather than blame or loud confidence, and trusts it enough to have Amandeep teach it to the club.

grounding: A coach's note shows a leader asking each member for a concern after a failure and scoring ideas on cost, time and feasibility.

Saturday

Our first bird feeder design failed on Tuesday. Squirrels ate everything in an hour. Everyone had agreed with Vandana's idea because she spoke first and loudest. I did too.

So today, as leader, I tried something different. I asked everyone to say one worry about any design before we chose. Out loud, one by one.

Vandana went first and said her own design was too open. Then Rishi said the second idea needed wood we couldn't afford. Kavita worried about time because of exams.

Then I made a quick table in my notebook: cost, time, will it work. Scores from one to five. The hanging bottle feeder won, and it was Kavita's quiet idea from Tuesday that nobody had listened to.

I'm Minakshi, and I felt nervous running it that way. But it felt fairer, and less like a popularity vote.

qa.q: How long did it take squirrels to eat everything?
qa.a: Squirrels ate everything in an hour.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel while running the new process?
qa.a: Minakshi felt nervous running the meeting a new way, but also that it was fairer.

qa.q: What could Minakshi try if some members still stay quiet?
qa.a: Minakshi could ask everyone to write their worry on a slip first, so shy members do not have to speak against louder ones.

qa.q: How might Kavita see the new way of choosing?
qa.a: Kavita probably feels seen and quietly pleased, since the idea ignored on Tuesday finally won on its merits.

grounding: A diary shows a leader, after a failure, asking each member for a concern and scoring ideas on cost, time and feasibility.
